chapter_title: The Adapter Pattern: Bridging Incompatible Interfaces

screens.title: The Adapter Pattern: Bridging Incompatible Interfaces
screens.subtitle: Use an Adapter to let modern code talk to legacy or third‑party components without changing either side.

narration.text: Imagine you arrive in a foreign country with a travel plug that won’t fit the wall socket. You could rebuild the device plug or change the building wiring, but the practical choice is a small travel adapter that translates one shape to another. In software, the Adapter pattern plays the same role. It provides a thin translator between a client’s expected interface and an existing class that exposes a different interface. In this chapter you will learn why this keeps your application code clean, how to implement the common Object Adapter in C#, and how to avoid turning adapters into over‑complicated gateways. You will see a concrete example where an ILogger interface is satisfied by a LegacyLogger with incompatible methods through a LegacyLoggerAdapter. We’ll also cover the less practical Class Adapter approach and its limits in C#, common mistakes like over‑adapting, and safety notes when integrating legacy components. By the end, you should be ready to identify adapter opportunities and to implement, test, and maintain lean adapters that preserve separation of concerns.

keyIdea.text: An Adapter translates one interface into another so a client can use an existing class without modification.

screens.title: What the Adapter pattern is — definition and analogy
screens.subtitle: A translator object that implements the Target interface and delegates to the Adaptee

narration.text: The Adapter pattern is a structural design pattern whose purpose is to let two incompatible interfaces collaborate by inserting a translator between them. Define three roles: the Target is the interface your client expects; the Adaptee is an existing class with a different A P I; and the Adapter implements the Target and uses the Adaptee to perform work. An easy analogy is a travel power adapter: it doesn’t change the device or the outlet, it translates the plug so they connect. In practice you implement an Adapter class that implements the expected interface and forwards or transforms calls to the Adaptee. For example, a client expects an ILogger with LogMessage, while a legacy library exposes WriteToConsole. The adapter receives LogMessage calls and internally calls WriteToConsole on the legacy instance. A common misconception is thinking the adapter fixes design problems inside the Adaptee. It doesn’t — it only provides compatibility. If the Adaptee has bugs or side effects, those remain and must be tested when you create the adapter. Keep adapters focused: one Adapter per translation responsibility. To check understanding: can you state the three roles and explain why composition is usually preferred in C#? That question helps lock in the core idea.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Adapter implements the Target and delegates to the Adaptee, acting as a translator without modifying either party.

content.html:
Core Concept
Adapter pattern defined
Three roles: Target, Adapter, Adaptee. Adapter translates calls to make collaboration possible.
Target
The interface the client expects, for example ILogger with LogMessage(string).
Adapter
Implements Target and calls methods on the Adaptee, performing translations as needed.
Adaptee
An existing class with an incompatible interface, such as LegacyLogger with WriteToConsole.
Key Takeaway

The adapter is a focused translator: it should not fix Adaptee internals or become a catch‑all for unrelated behavior.

Analogy: travel power adapter
Your device plug is unchanged, the outlet stays the same. The travel adapter simply translates the physical connection so power flows. In software, translation maps method names, parameters, and sometimes data structures.
Concrete example
Client expects ILogger.LogMessage(string). Legacy library exposes LegacyLogger.WriteToConsole(string). The adapter implements ILogger and calls the LegacyLogger method inside LogMessage.
Common misconception
Adapters are not a cure for poor legacy design. They enable use without changing the Adaptee, but you still must test and handle side effects from the legacy code.

screens.title: How to implement an Object Adapter in C#
screens.subtitle: Step‑by‑step composition-based adapter construction and validation

narration.text: Implementing an Object Adapter in C# follows a clear sequence. Step one: define the Target interface your client uses, for example ILogger with LogMessage. Step two: identify the Adaptee — the existing class whose A P I differs, such as LegacyLogger with WriteToConsole and WriteToFile methods. Step three: create an Adapter class that implements the Target and holds a reference to an Adaptee instance through constructor injection. Step four: implement Target methods by translating parameters and delegating to the Adaptee methods; include logging or transformation if the Adaptee names or parameter types differ. Step five: add defensive checks and tests. For instance, validate injected Adaptee is not null and write unit tests that assert the adapter calls the expected Adaptee methods with correctly transformed data. Practical validation prevents surprises when the legacy component has side effects. A common error is over‑translating: adding unrelated responsibilities or state to the adapter. Keep it thin and document the mapping rules. When you finish, the Application consumes ILogger and remains oblivious to the legacy implementation. Try to implement one adapter per Adaptee-to-Target translation and keep tests focused on the translation contract.

keyIdea.title: Implementation steps
keyIdea.text: Define Target, identify Adaptee, implement Adapter with composition, translate calls, and test the mapping thoroughly.

content.html:
Process Flow
Steps to build an object adapter
1. Define Target
Choose the interface the client expects, such as ILogger.LogMessage(string).
2. Identify Adaptee
Find the existing class to reuse, like LegacyLogger with a different method shape.
3. Implement Adapter
Implement Target and hold the Adaptee instance via constructor injection.
4. Translate and delegate
Map Target calls to Adaptee calls, transforming parameters as required.
5. Test and document
Add unit tests for translation logic and document mapping rules to avoid surprises.
Example validation checks
  • Ensure the injected Adaptee is non-null and behaves as expected.
  • Test that calls to LogMessage produce the correct Adaptee calls.
  • Guard against Adaptee side effects with integration tests.
Concrete scenario
Client expects ILogger.LogMessage. LegacyLogger exposes WriteToConsole(string) and WriteToFile(string). The Adapter maps LogMessage to WriteToConsole and can optionally add routing logic if needed.
Design rule
Adapters should not expand responsibilities; keep them focused on interface translation only.
Key Takeaway
Follow a stepwise process and validate with tests; composition gives you flexibility in C#.

screens.title: Live-code: ILogger and LegacyLoggerAdapter
screens.subtitle: Review the minimal C# implementation that adapts a legacy logger

narration.text: Now we will walk through a minimal, practical adapter implementation in C#. The Target is ILogger with a LogMessage method. The Adaptee is LegacyLogger providing WriteToConsole and WriteToFile. The Adapter class implements ILogger, holds a LegacyLogger instance injected in its constructor, and in LogMessage it logs an adapter message and forwards the payload to WriteToConsole. In this pattern the Application only depends on ILogger, so swapping different adapters or real loggers is simple. When you read the code, notice two important details: first, constructor injection ensures testability and allows you to substitute test doubles; second, the adapter may perform small translations or annotations before delegating. A common misunderstanding is to put business logic into the adapter. Avoid that. Keep the adapter responsible only for compatibility. After this walkthrough, write unit tests that mock the Adaptee and assert the adapter calls the expected methods. That practice ensures the legacy library’s behavior does not silently change your application's runtime behavior. keyIdea.title: Code rules
keyIdea.text: Use constructor injection and keep translation logic minimal; test against the Adaptee's expected calls.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Interfaces and legacy class
// The Target interface that our client expects
public interface ILogger
{
  void LogMessage(string message);
}

// The Adaptee: a legacy logging component with an incompatible interface
public class LegacyLogger
{
  public void WriteToConsole(string text)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"[LEGACY LOG]: {text}");
  }

  public void WriteToFile(string data)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"[LEGACY FILE LOG]: Saving '{data}' to file...");
  }
}
Adapter implementation
// The Adapter class
public class LegacyLoggerAdapter : ILogger
{
  private readonly LegacyLogger _legacyLogger;

  public LegacyLoggerAdapter(LegacyLogger legacyLogger)
  {
    _legacyLogger = legacyLogger ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(legacyLogger));
  }

  public void LogMessage(string message)
  {
    Console.WriteLine("Adapter translating message...");
    _legacyLogger.WriteToConsole(message);
  }
}

// Client wiring example
LegacyLogger legacy = new LegacyLogger();
ILogger adapter = new LegacyLoggerAdapter(legacy);
// Application code depends only on ILogger
Example note
The adapter logs a small message and delegates to the Adaptee. Unit tests should mock LegacyLogger and assert WriteToConsole is called with the expected text.

screens.title: How adapter composition affects architecture
screens.subtitle: Why composition gives flexibility and how adapters fit into clean architecture

narration.text: Adapters sit at a boundary: they decouple client code from the concrete implementations behind a known interface. When you place an Adapter between the client and a legacy Adaptee, the client depends only on the Target interface. Composition — the Adapter holding an Adaptee instance — preserves loose coupling and testability. This approach enables you to replace or wrap multiple Adaptees with different adapters without changing client code. Architecturally, adapters are often implemented in an integration layer or an adapter package to keep translation concerns separate from domain logic. One mistake is scattering adapters throughout domain services; that makes maintenance hard. Another architectural point: Class Adapters, which rely on inheritance, are less practical in C# because it lacks multiple inheritance of classes. That forces composition in most real systems. When designing your adapter layer, document mapping rules, keep adapters thin, and ensure tests verify both the translation and any side effects. Ask yourself: does this adapter make integration simpler without hiding defects? If the answer is yes, proceed; if it masks deeper design issues, consider refactoring instead. How adapter composition affects architecture means adapters belong in an integration layer; composition preserves testability and allows multiple adaptees to be adapted independently.. In practical terms, why composition gives flexibility and how adapters fit into clean architecture. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Architectural role
keyIdea.text: Adapters belong in an integration layer; composition preserves testability and allows multiple Adaptees to be adapted independently.

content.html:
Architecture
Adapter as an integration layer
Adapters decouple client code from concrete dependencies, preserving a stable boundary for your domain logic.
Client
Depends on Target interface only.
Adapter
Holds Adaptee via composition; translates calls.
Adaptee
Legacy or third‑party component with a different API.
Design guidance
  • Place adapters in an integration boundary, not scattered through domain services.
  • Prefer composition for testability and reusability.
  • Document mapping rules and side effects for maintainability.
Practical note
Class Adapters require inheritance and are constrained in C#. Composition lets a single adapter wrap different Adaptees or support multiple implementations more easily.
When to refactor instead
If interface mismatches indicate a systemic design issue, consider refactoring instead of adding many adapters.
Key Takeaway

Use adapters at integration boundaries; keep them small and test their translations to protect your domain logic.

screens.title: Object Adapter vs Class Adapter
screens.subtitle: Why object adapters are the common choice in C#

narration.text: It’s helpful to compare the Object Adapter and Class Adapter variants so you understand why C# developers usually pick composition. The Object Adapter holds an instance of the Adaptee and delegates calls to it. This favors composition, supports adapting multiple Adaptees, and is compatible with C#’s single inheritance model. The Class Adapter uses inheritance to adapt by deriving from the Adaptee and implementing the Target interface, which can be useful in languages with multiple inheritance, but it tightly couples the adapter to a particular Adaptee class. In C#, class adapters are rarely practical because you cannot inherit from two concrete classes at once. A common misconception is that class adapters are always simpler; in practice they reduce flexibility and testability. Object Adapters make it easy to inject mocks or substitutes in tests because the Adaptee is held via a field or property. When you must adapt several different Adaptees to the same Target, object adapters let you write multiple small adapters or a configurable adapter that wraps different instances. Prefer composition, keep responsibilities single, and choose class adapter only when inheritance semantics and language features clearly favor it.

keyIdea.title: Why composition
keyIdea.text: Object Adapter uses composition, enabling flexibility and testability; Class Adapter is limited in C# due to inheritance constraints.

content.html:
Comparison
Object Adapter
Composition: the Adapter holds an Adaptee instance and delegates calls. This approach is flexible, testable, and common in C#.
Pros
  • Supports multiple Adaptees
  • Testable via constructor injection
  • Does not require multiple inheritance
Comparison
Class Adapter
Inheritance: the Adapter inherits from the Adaptee and implements the Target. This can be limiting in C# and ties the adapter to one Adaptee.
Limitations
  • Tight coupling to a specific Adaptee class
  • Multiple inheritance constraints make it impractical in C#
  • Harder to mock in unit tests
Key Takeaway

In C#, object adapters using composition are the practical and testable choice; reserve class adapters only for languages where multiple inheritance makes them natural.

screens.title: Common mistakes and best practices
screens.subtitle: Keep adapters focused, test translations, and avoid over‑adapting

narration.text: When using adapters, watch for a few recurring mistakes. The first is over‑adapting: creating adapters for tiny, trivial mismatches instead of applying a small refactor or an extension method. Overuse of adapters adds indirection and maintenance cost. Second, do not let adapters accumulate unrelated responsibilities. An adapter should only translate interfaces; complex business logic belongs in the domain layer. Third, failing to test adapters is risky. Because adapters touch legacy code, you must verify both the translation mapping and any side effects the Adaptee may have. Unit tests that mock the Adaptee and integration tests that run the adapter against the real legacy component are both valuable. Best practices include constructor injection for testability, clear mapping documentation in comments or README, and keeping adapters in a dedicated integration package or layer so domain services remain uncluttered. Finally, when integrating legacy libraries, treat adapter development as an opportunity to identify design smells — sometimes a larger refactor is the better long‑term investment than many small adapters. Common mistakes and best practices means avoid over‑adapting, document the translation, and test both unit and integration paths to protect the system from legacy side effects.. In practical terms, keep adapters focused, test translations, and avoid over‑adapting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practice rules
keyIdea.text: Avoid over‑adapting, document the translation, and test both unit and integration paths to protect the system from legacy side effects.

content.html:
Best Practices
Keep adapters simple and tested
  • Use constructor injection to enable mocking and substitution.
  • Document the mapping between Target methods and Adaptee methods.
  • Write unit tests for translation logic and integration tests for side effects.
  • Place adapters in a dedicated integration layer for maintainability.
Common mistakes
These mistakes increase complexity or hide real design issues.
Over-adapting
Creating adapters for trivial mismatches instead of small refactors.
God adapter
Giving a single adapter too many unrelated responsibilities.
Key Takeaway

Prefer focused, documented adapters and test both the translation and the Adaptee integration to avoid hidden failures.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember about the Adapter pattern

narration.text: To wrap up, remember these compact concepts. The Adapter Pattern is a translator that allows objects with incompatible interfaces to collaborate. The Target is the interface the client expects; the Adaptee is the existing class you want to reuse; and the Adapter implements the Target and delegates to the Adaptee. In C#, the Object Adapter using composition is the practical choice: it supports testability and flexibility. Keep adapters focused on translation, avoid over‑adapting, and document mapping rules. Finally, always test adapters both in isolation and with the real legacy component so side effects are discovered early. These principles will help you integrate legacy or third‑party systems while keeping your application architecture clean and maintainable.
